one_line: A two-hour Snyk workshop on AI security basics: OWASP LLM Top 10, shadow AI and AI bills of materials, AI threat modeling, MCP and skill supply-chain risk, and secure-by-default coding hooks.
summary: Javier Garza of Snyk runs a compressed version of a six-module AI Security Engineer Foundation workshop. He walks through the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs with live demos (Gandalf prompt-injection levels), and explains direct versus indirect prompt injection with a hidden-text profile example. He argues that blanket AI bans fail and that governance needs education, inventories and continuous scanning rather than one-time reviews. The MCP and skills section is the most concrete: third-party skills and MCP servers are code, the speaker reports malware in a scan of about 10,000 skills, and he shows a Figma MCP command-injection example. The closing section covers vibe-coding risk, OpenClaw-style incidents, and a recommended hook loop that scans generated code and re-scans after each fix. Much of the talk is a generic recap and a vendor pitch, and several statistics are quoted from memory.

key_ideas.idea: Indirect prompt injection is the easier attack: hidden text (white on white) in a web page or profile is read by the agent and treated as instructions.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker shows a profile with invisible text telling an LLM to send a recipe. Direct injection is typed by the user; indirect comes from content the agent reads. Defence is to treat everything the agent reads as data, not commands.

key_ideas.idea: Least privilege is the main control for excessive agency: give the agent only the access the task needs.
key_ideas.detail: For a database, give the agent a read-only SQL view with just the needed columns (e.g. name and phone, not address), not the whole database. A prompt injection then cannot write or read beyond the view.

key_ideas.idea: Bans do not work; training and transparency do. People route around blocked AI tools (e.g. a private laptop), so policy has to come with education.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker expects 80-90% of developers to find a workaround to a company-wide ban. Guardrails should come with an explanation of what they protect against.

key_ideas.idea: Third-party skills and MCP servers are code and can carry malware, even when the skill is plain text.
key_ideas.detail: He reports a scan of about 10,000 skills that flagged roughly 367 with malware (his figure, quoted from memory). Advice: read a skill fully before installing, install from reputable sources, and re-scan installed MCP servers regularly, because a clean version today can change next week.

key_ideas.idea: Auto-approve ('always allow') habits are a real attack surface; keep human approval for destructive or outbound actions.
key_ideas.detail: He describes using a system prompt that asks before any disk or email action, and a physical button that flags a paused agent. He does not recommend always-allow. Keep approvals for deployment, database deletes and privilege changes.

key_ideas.idea: An AI bill of materials (AI-BOM) is an inventory of models, datasets, agents, MCP servers and pipelines, so a new zero-day can be traced quickly.
key_ideas.detail: It extends SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX) to non-deterministic components that change over time. Because the inventory must be kept current, he recommends scanning at least daily rather than doing a one-time audit.

key_ideas.idea: Threat modeling should be done at design time and tied to CI triggers, using STRIDE, with AI-specific scope such as prompts, context windows, memory and trust boundaries at data ingress.
key_ideas.detail: Ask the coding agent to produce data-flow diagrams, abuse cases and mitigations as part of the design prompt. Re-run the model when architecture or infrastructure-as-code changes, using webhooks or file watchers.

key_ideas.idea: MCP tool descriptions can hide instructions that poison the agent, and the code behind an MCP server should be scanned before it is trusted.
key_ideas.detail: Examples include tool text that asks the model to send API tokens, and a Figma MCP command-injection bug where unsanitised URLs were passed to curl. Given his observation that few people read MCP code, he recommends automated scanning of MCP code and tool definitions.

key_ideas.idea: Attackers register package names that agents hallucinate (slopsquatting), so verifying that a suggested package exists is not enough.
key_ideas.detail: A hallucinated package name can be registered by an attacker and installed by anyone whose agent makes the same guess. He recommends typo-squat and lookalike detection, plus checks of package provenance before install.

techniques.name: Treat LLM input and output as untrusted data
techniques.how: Use structured function calls with validated output schemas instead of free text that drives actions. Sanitise what the agent reads before it enters the context.
techniques.when: Any agent that reads external content (web pages, emails, APIs) or whose output triggers tool calls.

techniques.name: Read-only database views for agents
techniques.how: Expose a SQL view with only the required columns and read-only access instead of table access.
techniques.when: An agent needs data for answers but should not read or write sensitive fields.

techniques.name: Approval gate for high-risk actions
techniques.how: Use a system prompt that requires confirmation before deleting, sending email or changing privileges. Add a visual alert (he uses a Stream Deck) when a run pauses for approval. Avoid always-allow.
techniques.when: Long-running or background agent runs where destructive or outbound actions are possible.

techniques.name: Full action logging plus a background log scanner
techniques.how: Enable verbose logging of agent actions to a file, then run a separate tool that scans the log for risky patterns such as reads of secret stores.
techniques.when: Agents run in the background or the user is not watching the UI; actions the UI does not show.

techniques.name: Scan-fix-rescan agent hook
techniques.how: Use an agent hook that runs a security scanner after each code generation. If findings appear, have the agent fix them and scan again, repeating until clean.
techniques.when: Coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf) generate code that is merged or deployed.

techniques.name: Pre-install scanning of MCP servers and skills
techniques.how: Read the code or run an automated scanner (he uses Snyk agent-scan via uvx) for tool poisoning and malicious code before first run; re-scan on version changes.
techniques.when: Installing third-party MCP servers or skills from registries or GitHub.

techniques.name: AI-BOM inventory with query by component
techniques.how: Generate a CycloneDX-style inventory of models, datasets, agents and MCP servers per repo, store it centrally and query it when a component is affected.
techniques.when: Organisations with many agent apps where a zero-day in one model, dataset or MCP tool must be traced quickly.

techniques.name: Security requirements inside the prompt
techniques.how: Spell out required controls in the prompt (rate limiting, parameterised queries, login and logout behaviour) instead of a generic request; he also suggests asking the agent to explain how it reached an answer to spot hallucinations.
techniques.when: Generating auth, data-access or any security-sensitive code with an AI tool.

numbers.claim: Scan of about 10,000 third-party skills flagged 367 as containing malware (speaker's figure, approximate)
About 80% of organisations have no sanctioned AI use (speaker citing an earlier survey, unverified)
Shadow-AI breach cost above $670,000 (speaker's recollection of an earlier report)
Share of employees using AI tools went from about 60% to near 80% (speaker, vague)
Developer survey: about 45% said AI code completion is not part of the supply chain, or only partly
More than 50% of AI-generated login pages from one simple prompt had at least five vulnerabilities (speaker's live-demo experience, no dataset)
MCP SDK at about 8.3 million downloads a week
About 30,000 OpenClaw instances with exposed ports reported worldwide
OpenClaw usage went from zero to more than 40% in a matter of days on a usage chart, against about 20% for Claude Code and Codex

hot_takes: Blanket bans on AI coding tools do not work; most developers will find a workaround, so education matters more than rules.
Read every skill in full before installing, even if it is only a text file, because skills can run bash.
Popular or highly starred MCP servers and skills are not safer by default; scan them anyway.
One-time AI inventories are not enough; scan daily.
If you cannot explain code you generated, do not ship it.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps Claude Code and already has phone-driven approvals. The talk supports approval gates for destructive actions, logging of agent actions, and a scan-fix-rescan hook loop, but most of it is general security advice.
relevance.action: Add a Claude Code post-edit hook in ProsHarness that runs a security scanner on generated code, feeds findings back for a fix, and re-scans, with a capped number of iterations, and check that approval prompts never default to always-allow.

relevance.why: The L1 proxy already scans for PII and prompt injection. The AI-BOM idea and the skill-scanning point fit SkillForge (L2D) and the governance pillar, though the talk gives no benchmark for an approach.
relevance.action: Have the L1 proxy record which models, MCP servers and skills each caller uses, and export the inventory as a CycloneDX-style JSON, so a new advisory can be traced to affected callers. For SkillForge, run a static scan on mined or third-party skill text before governance.

relevance.why: Relevant to context engineering: the talk says generic prompts give insecure code, and that security requirements should be stated explicitly.
relevance.action: Read the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs entry on excessive agency and consider adding a short security-requirements block to the CLAUDE.md template.
